name: Design Patterns in Java

beginner.content:
Singleton Pattern ensures that only one object of a class is created in the entire application.

Real-Life Example:

  • Database Connection
  • Printer Spooler
  • Configuration Manager

Why do we need Singleton?

  • To save memory
  • To maintain global access
  • To control object creation

Basic Rules:

  • Private constructor
  • Static instance variable
  • Public static method to get instance

intermediate.content:
The Singleton Pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.

Why?

In the above program, we have created the 3 instance of same class but I want to create only 1 instance of class then I should go for singleton design pattern.

When?

If you have business requirement in which only 1 object is created then you should go for singleton design pattern.

Steps to create the singleton design pattern as


Step- 1 : Create class singleton and static member of class.
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class Singleton {
private static Singleton singletonobject;
}

Step- 2 : Make constructor as private
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class Singleton {
private static Singleton singletonobject;
private singleton(){
}
}

Step- 3 : Create the method for checking the references and use synchronized block instead of method.
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public static Singleton getSingletonObject() {
synchronized (Singleton.class) {
if (singletonobject == null) {
singletonobject = new Singleton();
} else {
return singletonobject;
}
return singletonobject;
}
}

Step- 4 : We can still able to create the copy of object by cloning it using object clone method.
Override the object clone method to prevent cloning as below.
(If singleton class will implements clonable interface ->class Singleton implements Clonable and override object clone method into singleton class)
public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
Singleton obj1 = Singleton.getSingletonObject();
Singleton obj2 = (Singleton) obj1.clone();
System.out.println("object 1>>"+obj1.hashCode());
System.out.println("object 2>>"+obj2.hashCode());
}
OUTPUT=object 1>>2018699554
object 2>>1311053135
This again violates the design principle. We need to override the object clone method which throws
CloneNotSupportedException.
@Override
protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
// TODO Auto-generated method stub
throw new CloneNotSupportedException("Singleton cannot be cloned"); // super.clone() would NOT prevent cloning
}
OUTPUT=object 1>>2018699554
object 2>>1311053135

Singleton Pattern with Serialization

Some times in distributed system, we need to implement serializable interface in singleton class so that we can store it state in file system and retrieve it later point.
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
import java.io.Serializable;
public class Singleton implements Cloneable, Serializable {
private static Singleton singletonobject;
private Singleton() {
}
public static Singleton getSingletonObject() {
synchronized (Singleton.class) {
if (singletonobject == null) {
singletonobject = new Singleton();
} else {
return singletonobject;
}
return singletonobject;
}
}
@Override
protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
// TODO Auto-generated method stub
return super.clone();
}
}

Step- 2 : Create class singleton with serialization
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.ObjectInput;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import java.io.ObjectOutput;
import java.io.ObjectOutputStream;
import java.io.Serializable;
public class SingletonSerializedTest implements Serializable {
private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
public static void main(String[] args) {
try {
Singleton instance1 = Singleton.getSingletonObject();
ObjectOutput out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("E:\test.txt"));
out.writeObject(instance1);
out.close();
ObjectInput in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("E:\test.txt"));
Singleton instance2 = (Singleton) in.readObject();
in.close();
System.out.println("instance 1>>" + instance1.hashCode());
System.out.println("instance 2>>" + instance2.hashCode());
} catch (Exception e) {
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
}

Step- 3 : Create the input and output for reading and writing the object .
ObjectOutput out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("D:\test.txt"));
out.writeObject(instance1);
out.close();
// deserailize from file to object
ObjectInput in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("D:\test.txt"));
Singleton instance2 = (Singleton) in.readObject();
in.close();

Step- 4 : Run program to check output.
instance1 hashCode:- 625576447
instance2 hashCode:- 1494279232

It is prove that singleton object is not preserved during deserialization. Because both instance have different hashcode.

Step- 5 : To overcome this problem, we need to override the readResolve() method into singleton class.
protected Object readResolve() {
return singletonobject;
}

Step- 6 : After Running SingletonSerializedTest Program, you will get the output as
instance1 hashCode:- 625576447
instance2 hashCode:- 625576447

expert.content:
Thread-Safe Singleton (Double Checked Locking)

This ensures only one instance is created even in multithreaded environment.

Bill Pugh Singleton Implementation (Best Practice)

Uses inner static helper class. Thread-safe without synchronized.

Singleton Using Enum (Most Secure Way)

✔ Prevents reflection attack
✔ Prevents serialization issue
✔ Prevents cloning issue
✔ Thread-safe by default

Common Singleton Issues & Solutions

  • Reflection: Can break singleton → Use enum
  • Serialization: Use readResolve()
  • Cloning: Override clone() method
  • Multithreading: Use Double Checked Locking or Bill Pugh

When NOT to use Singleton?

  • When dependency injection is better
  • When class has state changes frequently
  • When testing requires multiple instances

beginner.content:
Factory Design Pattern is used to create objects without exposing object creation logic to the client.

Simple Meaning:

Instead of using new keyword everywhere, we create objects using a Factory class.


Why Factory Pattern?

  • Removes tight coupling
  • Centralizes object creation
  • Makes code cleaner

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create Interface
  • Step 2: Create Concrete Classes
  • Step 3: Create Factory Class
  • Step 4: Call Factory from Client

Real Life Example:

Shape Factory → Circle, Rectangle, Square

intermediate.content:
Design the factory method in which multiple objects are stored called as Factory Design Pattern.
• The Factory Design Pattern is a Creational Pattern that provides an interface for creating objects but allows subclasses or methods to decide which class to instantiate.
• It promotes loose coupling by removing the need to bind application-specific classes into code.

Key Points

• Encapsulates Object Creation → Centralized place for creating objects.
• Loose Coupling → Client code doesn’t know which class it gets, only the interface.
• Promotes Reusability & Flexibility → Easy to add new product types.
• Return Common Interface / Superclass → Factory method returns a parent type.
• Real-Life Example → IRCTC Website.

Advantages

• Centralized object creation.
• Reduces tight coupling.
• Makes code more maintainable & scalable.

Disadvantages

• Adds extra classes (slightly more complexity).
• Sometimes makes debugging harder due to indirect instantiation.

Why?

• Sometime our application or frameworks don’t know what kind of object has to create at run time.
It only knows when it has to create.
• Another issue is that class will contain object of another classes, this can be easily achieved by just using the new keyword and the class constructor. The problem with this approach is that it is very hard coded approach to create the object as this creates dependency between two classes.
To overcome this above situation, we should go for factory pattern.

When?

When user wants the specific object at run time.

Example

Suppose we have requirement to book AC ticket for First tier, second tier and Third tier.
Step 1: Create the interface Booking.
Step 2: Create the concreate class First tier will implement the same interface.
Step 3: Create the concreate class Second tier will implement the same interface.
Step 4: Create the concreate class Third tier will implement the same interface.
Step 5: Create class BookingFactory to generate the object of concreate class.
Step 6: Create the factory class to get the object of concreate class by passing the data.

Step 1: Create the interface Booking
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public interface Booking { // Step: 01
public String getACClass();
}

Step 2: Create the concreate class First tier will implement the same interface
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class FirstTier implements Booking {
@Override
public String getACClass() {
return "first class-AC- Seat availability:10";
}
}

Step 3: Create the concreate class Second tier will implement the same interface
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class SecondTier implements Booking {
@Override
public String getACClass() {
return "Second class- AC- Seat availability:8";
}
}

Step 4: Create the concreate class Third tier will implement the same interface
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class ThirdTier implements Booking {
@Override
public String getACClass() {
return "Third class-AC Seat availability:2";
}
}

Step 5: Create class BookingFactory to generate the object of concreate class.
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
public class BookingFactory {
// Design the factory method here
// We Takes input should be first, second, third
public static Booking createBooking(String input) {
if (input.equalsIgnoreCase("first")) {
return new FirstTier();
} else if (input.equalsIgnoreCase("second")) {
return new SecondTier();
} else if (input.equalsIgnoreCase("third")) {
return new ThirdTier();
}
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid input from user..");
}
}

Step 6: Create the factory class to get the object of concreate class by passing the data.
package com.javaschoollab.demo;
import java.util.Scanner;
public class TestMain {
public static void main(String[] args) {
try {
String booking;
System.out.println("Enter the AC class type>>");
Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
booking = scanner.next();
Booking b = BookingFactory.createBooking(booking);
System.out.println(b.getACClass());
scanner.close();
} catch (Exception e) {
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
}

OUTPUT
Enter the AC class type>>
first
first class-AC- Seat availability:10

expert.content:
Problem in Simple Factory

Using multiple if-else blocks violates Open Closed Principle (OCP). Every new type requires modifying factory class.

Solution: Use Polymorphism (Factory Method Pattern)

Factory Using Enum (Cleaner Approach)

Removes if-else and improves readability.

Factory Pattern in Frameworks

  • Spring → BeanFactory
  • Hibernate → SessionFactory
  • Java → Calendar.getInstance()
  • JDBC → DriverManager.getConnection()

When NOT to Use Factory?

  • When object creation is simple
  • When only one implementation exists

Factory vs Abstract Factory

  • Factory → Creates one product
  • Abstract Factory → Creates families of related products

Factory Pattern with Dependency Injection (Spring Example)

Modern applications rarely use manual factories. Instead, frameworks like Spring internally use Factory pattern with Dependency Injection.

How Spring Uses Factory?

  • BeanFactory
  • ApplicationContext
  • @Bean annotated methods

Spring container decides which object to create at runtime. Client only depends on interface.

Factory with Reflection (Dynamic Object Creation)

Instead of using if-else or switch, we can dynamically create objects using Reflection. This makes factory fully dynamic.

⚠️ Used in Frameworks & Libraries

Factory with Registry Pattern

Instead of modifying factory every time, we can register objects in Map. This follows Open Closed Principle properly.

Best for Scalable Systems

Thread-Safe Factory

If factory manages shared resources, it must be thread-safe.

Example:

Factory Pattern + SOLID Principles

How Factory Supports SOLID:

  • S - Single Responsibility → Object creation separated
  • O - Open Closed → Add new product without modifying client
  • L - Liskov Substitution → Subtypes replace parent type
  • D - Dependency Inversion → Depend on abstraction

Common Mistakes

  • Putting business logic inside factory
  • Using too many if-else blocks
  • Violating OCP
  • Creating God Factory class

Real Industry Use Cases

  • JDBC DriverManager → Returns driver implementation
  • Calendar.getInstance()
  • LoggerFactory in SLF4J
  • Spring BeanFactory
  • Hibernate SessionFactory
  • Microservices → Strategy selection based on config

Performance Consideration

  • Factory adds slight abstraction overhead
  • Reflection-based factory is slower
  • Best approach → Registry or Dependency Injection

Factory vs Factory Method vs Abstract Factory

Type Creates Complexity
Simple Factory One type of object Low
Factory Method Delegates creation to subclasses Medium
Abstract Factory Family of related objects High

Factory Method is a step towards Abstract Factory.

beginner.content:
Abstract Factory Pattern provides an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes - it's essentially a "factory of factories".

Real-Life Example:

  • A cross-platform UI toolkit that produces matching Button + Checkbox + ScrollBar for Windows OR macOS
  • A vehicle factory producing matching Engine + Tyres + Body for a Car OR a Bike

Why do we need Abstract Factory?

  • To ensure a group of related products are used together consistently (you never accidentally mix a Windows Button with a Mac Checkbox)
  • To keep client code independent of concrete product classes
  • To make swapping an entire "family" of products a one-line change

Factory Method vs Abstract Factory:

  • Factory Method creates ONE product via a single overridable method
  • Abstract Factory creates a FAMILY of related products via multiple methods on one factory interface

Builder Pattern constructs a complex object step by step, separating the construction process from the final representation - avoiding constructors with a huge number of parameters ("telescoping constructors").

Real-Life Example:

  • Building a House (foundation, walls, roof, paint - each step optional/configurable)
  • Building a Meal order (burger, with/without cheese, with/without fries, drink size)
  • Java's own StringBuilder and StringBuffer

Why do we need Builder?

  • To avoid constructors with 6, 8, 10+ parameters that are impossible to read at the call site
  • To make optional parameters truly optional, instead of forcing null placeholders
  • To make the object immutable once built
  • To read fluently: new Pizza.Builder().size(12).cheese(true).build()

Prototype Pattern creates new objects by copying (cloning) an existing object instead of building it from scratch - useful when object creation is expensive (heavy DB call, complex computation) but a near-identical copy is cheap.

Real-Life Example:

  • Photocopying a document instead of retyping it
  • Cloning a fully-configured game character/enemy template to spawn new instances
  • Java's own Object.clone() and the Cloneable interface

Why do we need Prototype?

  • To avoid re-running expensive initialization logic for every new object
  • To create objects without depending on their concrete class (works via an interface reference)
  • To easily produce variations of a "base" configured object

Shallow vs Deep Clone:

  • Shallow clone copies primitive fields directly but COPIES THE REFERENCE for object fields - both the original and the clone point to the SAME nested object
  • Deep clone recursively clones nested objects too, so the clone is fully independent

Adapter Pattern lets two incompatible interfaces work together by wrapping one of them in an object (the adapter) that translates calls between them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A travel plug adapter that lets a US plug fit into an Indian socket
  • A memory card reader that lets an SD card connect to a USB port
  • Java's own Arrays.asList() adapting an array to the List interface

Why do we need Adapter?

  • To reuse existing/legacy code that has an incompatible interface, without modifying it
  • To let two independently-developed classes collaborate
  • To integrate a third-party library's class into your own interface

Decorator Pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically, by wrapping it in decorator objects - a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending behavior.

Real-Life Example:

  • Coffee shop: base Coffee, then wrap it with Milk, then Sugar, then Whipped Cream - each adds cost/description
  • Java's own BufferedReader(new FileReader(...)) and InputStreamReader chains

Why do we need Decorator?

  • To add behavior to individual objects at RUNTIME, without affecting other instances of the same class
  • To avoid an explosion of subclasses for every combination of features (e.g. MilkSugarCoffee, SugarCreamCoffee, ...)
  • To keep each responsibility in its own small class (Single Responsibility Principle)

Facade Pattern provides a single, simplified interface in front of a complex subsystem made up of many interacting classes - the client talks only to the facade.

Real-Life Example:

  • A car's ignition button - one press ("start") hides fuel injection, spark plugs, starter motor, battery checks
  • A hotel "concierge" who coordinates room service, laundry, and cab booking behind one request

Why do we need Facade?

  • To hide the complexity of a subsystem with many classes behind one easy-to-use entry point
  • To reduce coupling between client code and a subsystem's internal classes
  • To provide a simpler, higher-level API without removing access to the underlying subsystem for advanced use cases

Proxy Pattern provides a placeholder/surrogate object that controls access to another (often expensive or remote) object - the proxy implements the same interface, so the client can't tell the difference.

Real-Life Example:

  • A credit card is a proxy for your bank account - it controls and checks access before money moves
  • A security guard checking ID before letting someone into a building (access control proxy)
  • Lazy-loading a huge image - a lightweight proxy stands in until the real image is actually needed

Why do we need Proxy?

  • Lazy initialization (Virtual Proxy): delay creating an expensive object until it's actually used
  • Access control (Protection Proxy): check permissions before delegating to the real object
  • Logging/Caching: add cross-cutting behavior around calls without changing the real object

The Bridge Pattern decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently - instead of one growing inheritance tree, you split it into two smaller, separately-extensible hierarchies connected by composition.

Real-Life Example:

  • A TV remote (abstraction) working with different TV brands (implementation) - the remote's buttons stay the same regardless of which brand it controls
  • A universal charger (abstraction) working with different phone brands' charging circuits
  • A payment app (abstraction) working with different payment gateway implementations

Why do we need Bridge?

  • When a class varies along two independent dimensions (e.g. shape type AND color), plain inheritance forces a subclass per combination (RedCircle, GreenCircle, RedSquare, GreenSquare...) - this explodes quickly
  • Bridge splits the two dimensions into separate hierarchies joined by a reference, so either side can grow without touching the other

expert.content:
Bridge vs Adapter

Both use composition and both involve an interface, but the intent differs: Adapter is applied after the fact to make two already-existing, incompatible interfaces work together; Bridge is designed up front so an abstraction and its implementation can be developed and extended independently from day one.

Real-World Usage

JDBC is a textbook real Bridge: your Java code programs against the abstraction (java.sql.Connection, Statement), while each database vendor ships its own driver as the implementation side - swapping MySQL for PostgreSQL never requires changing your application code.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Bridge solve?Class explosion when a type has two or more independently varying dimensions - it splits them into separate hierarchies joined by composition
Bridge vs Adapter - what's the real difference?Adapter retrofits incompatible interfaces after the fact; Bridge is designed up front to let abstraction and implementation evolve independently
Give a real JDK/framework example of BridgeJDBC - Connection/Statement is the abstraction, each vendor's driver is the implementation

beginner.content:
The Composite Pattern lets you treat individual objects and groups of objects through the same interface, so client code doesn't need to know whether it's dealing with a single item or a whole tree of them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A file system - a File and a Folder (which can contain Files and other Folders) both expose the same "get size" operation
  • An org chart - an individual employee and an entire department both respond to "list all members"
  • A UI toolkit - a single Button and a Panel full of widgets both respond to "render"

Why do we need Composite?

  • Represent part-whole (tree) hierarchies naturally
  • Let client code call the same method on a leaf or an entire branch without an if/else check for "is this one item or many?"

expert.content:
When to Use Composite

Reach for Composite whenever your domain is naturally a tree and you find yourself writing "if this is a single item, do X; if it's a group, loop and do X to each" - Composite eliminates that branch entirely by giving both cases the same interface.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What structural problem does Composite solve?Letting client code treat a single object and a group/tree of objects uniformly through one shared interface
Give an example of Composite in the JDKjava.awt.Container extends Component - a Container can hold other Components, including other Containers
What's the trade-off of Composite?Leaf-only operations (like "add child") must still exist on the shared interface even though a leaf can't meaningfully support them, unless you accept throwing UnsupportedOperationException

beginner.content:
The Flyweight Pattern reduces memory usage by sharing common state across many similar objects instead of storing that state redundantly in each one.

Real-Life Example:

  • A text editor - every occurrence of the letter "A" in a document can share ONE glyph/font object instead of each character owning its own copy
  • A game with thousands of trees on a map - the 3D model/texture (shared) is reused; only each tree's x/y position (unique) is stored per instance

Intrinsic vs Extrinsic State

  • Intrinsic state - shared, immutable, stored once inside the flyweight object (e.g. the character's font/shape)
  • Extrinsic state - unique per usage, passed in from outside at the point of use, NOT stored in the flyweight (e.g. the character's x/y position on screen)

expert.content:
A Built-In JDK Flyweight: Integer Caching

Integer.valueOf(int) caches and reuses Integer objects for values -128 to 127 - this is exactly the Flyweight idea baked into the JDK itself, which is why Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b is true, but the same comparison for 1000 is false (outside the cached range, a new object is created each time).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Flyweight solve?Excessive memory usage when creating a very large number of similar objects, by sharing their common (intrinsic) state instead of duplicating it
Difference between intrinsic and extrinsic state?Intrinsic state is shared and stored inside the flyweight; extrinsic state is unique per use and supplied by the caller at call time, never stored in the flyweight
Name a Flyweight example already in the JDKInteger.valueOf() caching Integer objects in the range -128 to 127

beginner.content:
Observer Pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects, so that when one object (the "subject") changes state, all its dependents ("observers") are notified and updated automatically.

Real-Life Example:

  • YouTube channel subscribers get notified whenever the channel uploads a new video
  • Newspaper/magazine subscription - all subscribers get the new edition automatically
  • Java's own java.util.Observer (legacy) and any GUI event-listener system

Why do we need Observer?

  • To notify multiple dependent objects about a state change without tightly coupling them to the subject
  • To let observers be added/removed at runtime without changing the subject's code
  • It's the foundation of event-driven and reactive programming (pub-sub systems)

Chain of Responsibility lets you pass a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides either to process the request or pass it to the next handler.

Real-Life Example:

  • ATM cash dispenser — handles request using 2000, 500, 100 notes in a chain
  • Tech support escalation — L1 support tries first, then L2, then L3
  • Leave approval — Manager approves small leaves, Director approves longer ones

Why do we need it?

  • Decouples sender of a request from its receivers
  • Multiple objects get a chance to handle the request
  • New handlers can be added without changing existing code

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create abstract Handler with a setNext() method
  • Step 2: Create concrete handlers that either handle or forward the request
  • Step 3: Client builds the chain and sends request to the first handler

expert.content:
ATM Cash Dispenser — Full Chain Example

A very common interview example: dispensing cash using the fewest number of currency notes, where each handler is responsible for one denomination and passes the remainder down the chain.

Servlet Filters — A Real Chain of Responsibility Example

The Java Servlet API's Filter mechanism is a textbook production use of Chain of Responsibility. Each filter processes the request/response and then decides whether to pass control to the next filter using FilterChain.doFilter().

Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator

Aspect Chain of Responsibility Decorator
Intent Pass request until someone handles it Add extra behavior/wrapping around an object
Execution Usually only ONE handler processes it (or a subset), can stop early Every decorator in the stack always executes
Structure Linked list of handlers Nested wrapper objects
Example Servlet Filters, Leave Approval, ATM Dispenser BufferedReader wrapping Reader, java.io streams

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to call next handler — request silently gets dropped
  • Creating a circular chain (A → B → A), leading to infinite loops
  • Not having a default/terminal handler that guarantees the request is eventually handled

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is Chain of Responsibility?A behavioral pattern that passes a request along a chain of handlers until one of them handles it
2What problem does it solve?Decouples the sender of a request from the specific object that will handle it
3Give a real Java framework example.Servlet Filters — each Filter decides whether to handle/modify the request and call chain.doFilter() to continue
4What's a common bug with this pattern?Forgetting to forward to the next handler, silently dropping the request
5Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator?CoR usually stops at the first handler that processes the request; Decorator always runs every wrapper in the stack
6How do you prevent infinite loops in a chain?Build the chain as a strict acyclic structure and always terminate with a handler that has next = null

beginner.content:
What is the Interpreter Pattern?

The Interpreter Pattern defines a way to evaluate language grammar or expressions. It represents each rule of the grammar as a class, and combines these classes to interpret sentences (expressions) in that language.

Real-Life Example:

  • A calculator that reads "3 + 5 * 2" and evaluates the result.
  • A traffic signal controller interpreting simple rule sentences like "IF car THEN stop".
  • A basic search engine interpreting boolean queries like "java AND spring".

Why do we need Interpreter Pattern?

  • To evaluate expressions written in a simple custom language or grammar.
  • To break a complex expression into smaller, manageable expression objects.
  • To make grammar rules easy to extend by adding new expression classes.

Basic Structure:

  • Expression (interface) — declares an interpret() method.
  • Terminal Expression — represents the basic elements of grammar (e.g., a number).
  • Non-Terminal Expression — represents rules combining other expressions (e.g., addition, multiplication).
  • Client — builds the expression tree and calls interpret().

How It Works — Step by Step

  • Every number (3, 5, 2) becomes a NumberExpression (Terminal Expression).
  • The multiplication "5 * 2" becomes a MultiplyExpression wrapping the two numbers.
  • The addition "3 + (5*2)" becomes an AddExpression wrapping the number and the multiply expression.
  • Calling interpret() on the outermost expression recursively evaluates the whole tree.

Expression Tree Diagram:

              AddExpression
              /           \\
      NumberExpression(3)   MultiplyExpression
                              /           \\
                    NumberExpression(5)  NumberExpression(2)

Each node "interprets itself" and passes the result up to its parent — this is a classic recursive tree evaluation.

expert.content:
Where Interpreter Pattern is Actually Used

  • Regex engines — a regular expression is compiled into a tree of terminal/non-terminal expressions and interpreted against input text.
  • SQL parsers — query language grammar (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN clauses) is parsed into an expression tree and interpreted/executed.
  • Rule engines — business rule engines (like Drools) interpret condition expressions such as "age > 18 AND country == 'IN'".
  • Spring Expression Language (SpEL) — @Value("#{someBean.someProperty}") is parsed and interpreted internally using this pattern.
  • Template engines — interpreting placeholders like {{ name }} in templates.

Terminal vs Non-Terminal Expressions

Type Meaning Example
Terminal Expression Leaf node of the grammar tree — cannot be broken down further NumberExpression, VariableExpression
Non-Terminal Expression Combines one or more other expressions to form a grammar rule AddExpression, MultiplyExpression, AndExpression, OrExpression

Why Interpreter is Rarely Used in Production

  • Performance: Deeply nested expression trees mean deeply nested recursive calls — this becomes slow for complex grammars.
  • Class explosion: Every grammar rule needs its own class, so a moderately complex language quickly results in dozens of expression classes.
  • Maintainability: Hand-written interpreters are hard to extend and debug compared to using a dedicated parsing tool.
  • Better alternatives exist: Real-world parsing needs (SQL, DSLs, config languages) are almost always solved using mature parser generator libraries like ANTLR, JavaCC, or existing libraries (e.g., javax.script, Spring's SpEL parser) instead of writing a hand-rolled Interpreter pattern.

When Interpreter Pattern IS still a reasonable choice

  • The grammar is very small and simple (a handful of rules).
  • The grammar is unlikely to grow significantly.
  • You need something quick and don't want the overhead of a full parser generator toolchain.

Interpreter vs Visitor Pattern

Aspect Interpreter Pattern Visitor Pattern
Purpose Evaluate/interpret a grammar or language expression Add new operations to an existing object structure without changing its classes
Where logic lives Each expression class implements its own interpret() logic Logic lives in a separate Visitor class, objects just accept() the visitor
Extending with new operations Hard - requires modifying/adding expression classes Easy - just add a new Visitor implementation

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is the Interpreter Pattern?A behavioral pattern that represents grammar rules as classes and evaluates expressions using an interpret() method
2What is a Terminal Expression?A leaf-level expression in the grammar that cannot be broken down further (e.g., a number or variable)
3What is a Non-Terminal Expression?An expression that combines other expressions to represent a grammar rule (e.g., addition, AND, OR)
4Give a real-world example of Interpreter usage.Regex engines, SQL parsers, rule engines, and Spring's SpEL expression evaluation
5Why is Interpreter rarely used in large production systems?Performance issues with deep recursion, class explosion for complex grammars, and better alternatives like ANTLR exist
6Interpreter vs Visitor pattern?Interpreter evaluates a grammar/language expression tree; Visitor adds new operations to an existing object structure without modifying it

beginner.content:
Iterator Pattern provides a way to access elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its underlying representation (array, list, tree, etc.).

Real-Life Example:

A TV remote lets you browse channels one by one using the "Next" / "Previous" buttons. You don't need to know whether the channels are stored as a list, an array, or fetched from a server - the remote just gives you one channel at a time.

Why do we need Iterator Pattern?

  • To traverse a collection without exposing its internal structure
  • To provide a uniform way of iterating over different types of collections
  • To support multiple simultaneous traversals of the same collection

Basic Structure:

  • Iterator - interface with hasNext() and next() methods
  • Concrete Iterator - implements traversal logic for a specific collection
  • Aggregate (Collection) - interface with a createIterator() method
  • Concrete Aggregate - returns a Concrete Iterator for itself

expert.content:
Java's Built-in Iterator and Iterable

The JDK already implements the Iterator pattern via java.util.Iterator and java.lang.Iterable. Implementing Iterable in your own class lets it be used directly in a for-each loop, integrating naturally with the rest of the Collections framework.

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators

Java Collections provide two categories of iterators depending on how they behave when the underlying collection is modified during iteration.

Aspect Fail-Fast Fail-Safe
Behavior on modification Throws ConcurrentModificationException immediately Iterates over a snapshot/copy, no exception
Underlying mechanism Uses an internal modCount checked on every next() Works on a cloned/copy-on-write structure
Examples ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentModificationException - Why It Happens

Fail-fast iterators (like those returned by ArrayList) track a modCount field on the collection. Every structural modification (add/remove) increments it. The iterator captures the modCount at creation and compares it on every call to next() - if they differ, it throws ConcurrentModificationException to warn you early rather than let the program silently misbehave.

Correct Way to Remove While Iterating

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is the Iterator Pattern?A behavioral pattern that lets you access elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its internal structure
2Where does Java implement this pattern natively?java.util.Iterator and java.lang.Iterable - implementing Iterable enables the for-each loop
3Why does removing an element in a for-each loop throw an exception?The for-each loop uses a fail-fast iterator internally; direct collection modification during iteration is detected via modCount and throws ConcurrentModificationException
4What's the safe way to remove elements while iterating?Use Iterator.remove() instead of Collection.remove(), which keeps modCount in sync
5Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators?Fail-fast throws ConcurrentModificationException on concurrent modification (ArrayList, HashMap); fail-safe iterates a snapshot/copy with no exception (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap)
6When would you prefer Stream API over Iterator?For bulk map/filter/reduce style processing, since Stream is more expressive than manual iteration

beginner.content:
Mediator Pattern defines an object that coordinates communication between a group of other objects, so they don't talk to each other directly.

Real-Life Example:

  • Air Traffic Control Tower — planes don't talk to each other directly, tower coordinates them
  • Chat Room — users send messages through a mediator, not directly to every other user
  • Airport Ground Staff Coordination

Why do we need it?

  • Without a mediator, every object needs a reference to every other object (many-to-many mess)
  • Mediator centralizes communication logic in one place
  • Reduces tight coupling between components

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create a Mediator interface
  • Step 2: Create a concrete mediator implementing coordination logic
  • Step 3: Colleague objects (e.g., User) hold a reference to the mediator only
  • Step 4: Colleagues communicate via the mediator, never directly

expert.content:
How Mediator Reduces Coupling

Without Mediator, N objects that need to talk to each other require up to N*(N-1) direct references — a many-to-many mesh of dependencies. With Mediator, every object needs only ONE reference — to the mediator — turning the relationship into many-to-one.
codeExamples:
Without Mediator:                With Mediator:

  A --- B                           A
  | \\ / |                          |
  |  X  |                          M --- B
  | / \\ |                          |
  C --- D                           C, D

expert.content:
Mediator vs Facade

Both patterns introduce an intermediary object, but their purpose is different.

Aspect Mediator Facade
Intent Coordinates two-way communication between colleague objects Provides a simplified one-way entry point to a subsystem
Colleagues aware of it? Yes — colleagues explicitly call the mediator No — subsystem classes don't know Facade exists
Example Chat room, Air traffic control Simplified API over multiple complex services

Real-World Use — GUI Frameworks & Event Buses

  • GUI frameworks — a Dialog acts as mediator between buttons, textboxes, checkboxes, so widgets don't reference each other directly
  • Event Bus / Message Bus (e.g., Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher) — publishers and subscribers don't know each other, the bus mediates
  • MVC Controllers — often act as mediators between View and Model components

Common Mistakes

  • Letting the mediator grow into a "God Object" containing all business logic
  • Colleague objects still holding direct references to each other "just in case"
  • Not splitting mediator responsibilities when it becomes too large — consider multiple smaller mediators

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is the Mediator Pattern?A behavioral pattern that centralizes communication between related objects through a single mediator instead of direct references
2What problem does it solve?Avoids a many-to-many mesh of direct dependencies between objects, replacing it with a many-to-one relationship to the mediator
3Mediator vs Observer?Mediator coordinates two-way communication between known colleagues; Observer is a one-to-many notification where the subject doesn't know what observers do with the update
4Mediator vs Facade?Mediator coordinates two-way communication colleagues are aware of; Facade simplifies one-way access to a subsystem the client is unaware of internally
5Give a real-world Java example.Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher acts as a mediator between event publishers and listeners
6What's the main risk of overusing Mediator?The mediator itself can grow into a "God Object" holding too much business logic

beginner.content:
Strategy Pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each one in its own class, and lets the client swap between them at runtime - without changing the code that uses them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A navigation app choosing between "fastest route", "shortest route", or "avoid tolls" strategies
  • A checkout page letting a customer pay by Credit Card, UPI, or PayPal - each is a different payment strategy
  • Java's own Comparator passed into Collections.sort(list, comparator)

Why do we need Strategy?

  • To eliminate long if-else/switch chains that pick behavior based on a type flag
  • To let each algorithm be tested, extended, and swapped independently (Open/Closed Principle)
  • To let the algorithm vary independently from the client that uses it

Command Pattern turns a request into a standalone object containing everything needed to perform an action (or undo it) - decoupling the object that invokes an operation from the object that knows how to perform it.

Real-Life Example:

  • A TV remote control - each button is a Command object that knows what device action to trigger
  • Restaurant order slips - a waiter writes a command that the kitchen executes later, independently
  • Undo/redo functionality in text editors

Why do we need Command?

  • To decouple the sender (the button/invoker) from the receiver (the object that does the actual work)
  • To support undo/redo by keeping a history of executed Command objects
  • To queue, log, or schedule requests as objects instead of executing them immediately

Template Method Pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method, deferring some of its individual steps to subclasses - the overall sequence stays fixed, but specific steps can be customized.

Real-Life Example:

  • Making tea vs coffee - both follow "boil water -> brew -> pour in cup -> add condiments", but "brew" and "add condiments" differ
  • A standardized exam-checking process where the overall flow is fixed but subject-specific grading differs

Why do we need Template Method?

  • To avoid duplicating the common parts of an algorithm across multiple subclasses
  • To enforce a fixed overall structure/sequence while still allowing customization of individual steps
  • To let subclasses override only what varies ("hook" methods) - this is the Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call you"

What is Memento Pattern?

Memento Pattern captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later - without violating encapsulation (no other object ever sees the fields being snapshotted directly).

Real-Life Example:

• A text editor's Undo feature - each save point remembers the document's exact content.
• A video game's checkpoint/save system - restoring a saved game returns the world to that exact state.

Why do we need Memento?

• To implement undo/redo without exposing an object's private internals to whoever manages the history.
• To let an object's state be saved and restored while keeping that state's representation private to the object itself.

The Three Roles

• Originator - the object whose state is being saved; creates a Memento and can restore itself from one.
• Memento - an immutable snapshot of the Originator's state at a point in time.
• Caretaker - stores Mementos (e.g. in a stack/history) but never looks inside them - it just hands them back to the Originator when asked.

expert.content:
Why Encapsulation Is Preserved

The EditorMemento's state is only readable by the TextEditor (Originator) that created it - the History (Caretaker) only ever calls push()/pop() and never touches getContent() itself. This is the entire point of the pattern: the Caretaker can manage when to save/restore without ever knowing what is being saved.

In stricter designs, the Memento class is made a private inner class of the Originator, or its state-reading method is package-private - so only the Originator's own package can access it at all.

Memento vs Command Pattern

Both patterns are commonly used to implement undo, but they capture different things:

AspectMementoCommand
What it storesA snapshot of state (data)An action/request (behavior), sometimes with its inverse
Undo mechanismRestore a previous snapshot directlyExecute a stored "undo" operation, or re-derive the prior state
Best fitState is small/cheap to snapshot wholesaleOperations are naturally reversible (e.g. insert -> delete)

In real editors, the two are often combined: a Command represents "what the user did," while a Memento captures the state needed to reverse it cleanly.

The Memory Cost Tradeoff

Storing a full snapshot on every change can get expensive for large objects. Real systems mitigate this by:
• Storing diffs/deltas instead of full copies where possible.
• Capping the undo history depth (discarding the oldest Mementos).
• Using structural sharing (immutable data structures) so unrelated parts of the state aren't duplicated.

Common Mistakes

• Letting the Caretaker read or mutate a Memento's internal fields - defeats the whole purpose of the pattern.
• Making Memento mutable - a later change to the "saved" state would corrupt every restore point that shares it.
• Snapshotting far more state than is actually needed to restore correctly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Memento solve?Capturing and restoring an object's internal state (for undo/checkpoints) without exposing that state's internal representation to outside code
What are the three roles in Memento?Originator (owns the state, creates/restores Mementos), Memento (the immutable snapshot), Caretaker (stores Mementos without inspecting them)
How does Memento preserve encapsulation?Only the Originator can read a Memento's internal state; the Caretaker just stores and returns opaque Memento objects
Memento vs Command for undo?Memento restores by replacing state with a saved snapshot; Command undoes by executing a stored reverse operation - they're often combined
What's the main downside of Memento?Memory cost - storing many full-state snapshots can be expensive, mitigated with diffs or a capped history size

beginner.content:
What is State Pattern?

State Pattern lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes - it looks to the outside world as if the object changed its class.

Real-Life Example:

• A Traffic Light - behaves differently in Red, Yellow, and Green states.
• An ATM Machine - behaves differently when a card is inserted vs when it isn't.
• A Media Player - Play, Pause, and Stop states each respond differently to the same button presses.

Why do we need State Pattern?

• Avoids huge if-else/switch blocks that branch on the current state everywhere in the code.
• Each state's behavior lives in its own dedicated class, instead of being scattered.
• New states can be added without touching any existing state class.

Basic Structure

• Step 1 - Create a State interface.
• Step 2 - Create concrete state classes implementing it.
• Step 3 - Create a Context class that holds a reference to the current state.
• Step 4 - The Context delegates behavior to whichever state object it currently holds.

expert.content:
State vs Strategy Pattern

State and Strategy look structurally identical (both plug an interface implementation into a context), but their intent differs:

AspectStateStrategy
IntentObject changes behavior as its internal state changesClient chooses which algorithm to use
Who switches implementationThe state objects themselves (self-transition)The client, from outside
AwarenessStates often know about each other / the next stateStrategies are independent, unaware of each other
ExampleATM, Traffic Light, Order statusComparator, Sorting algorithm, Payment method

Thread Lifecycle - A Real JDK Example of State

Java's Thread class is a great real-world analogy for the State pattern. A thread moves through states - NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED - and its allowed operations change depending on which state it's in, exactly like the ATM example.
• Thread.State enum represents the current state.
• The JVM internally manages transitions (you can't call start() twice, for example).
• The behavior of join()/interrupt() differs depending on the current state.

State Machine Libraries

For complex workflows (order processing, approval flows), hand-rolled State pattern classes can get unwieldy. Real projects often use dedicated state machine libraries instead:
• Spring Statemachine - declarative state/transition configuration for Spring apps.
• Squirrel State Machine - a lightweight Java state machine library.
• Enum-based state machines - using an EnumMap of allowed transitions.

Common Mistakes

• Putting transition logic in the Context instead of the State classes.
• Creating a new state object on every call instead of reusing singletons (as the ATM example does with hasCardState/noCardState).
• Forgetting to guard illegal transitions (e.g. requesting cash with no card inserted).

When NOT to Use State Pattern

• When there are only 2-3 simple states with trivial behavior - a simple flag/if-else may be enough.
• When states never change behavior, only data.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does State solve?Avoids scattered if-else/switch blocks by giving each state its own class, so an object's behavior changes cleanly as its state changes
State vs Strategy - what's the real difference?Same structure, different intent: State changes behavior driven by internal state transitions; Strategy lets the client pick an algorithm from outside
Who triggers a state transition?Typically the state objects themselves, by calling setState() on the context after handling a request
Give a real JDK example of the State pattern idea.Thread's lifecycle states (NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TERMINATED) - allowed operations differ per state
When should you avoid the State pattern?When there are only a couple of trivial states - a simple boolean/if-else is simpler and avoids unnecessary classes

beginner.content:
What is Visitor Pattern?

Visitor Pattern lets you add new operations to a group of classes without modifying those classes themselves.

Real-Life Example:

• A Tax Auditor - visits different account types (Savings, Current) and applies different rules to each, without the account classes knowing anything about tax rules.
• A Shopping Cart discount calculator - "visits" different item types (Book, Electronics) and applies different discount logic per type.

Why do we need it?

• Adding a new operation normally means modifying every element class to support it.
• Visitor moves that operation's logic into a separate Visitor class instead.
• Keeps the element classes stable while the set of operations can keep growing.

Basic Structure

• Step 1 - Create a Visitor interface with a visit() method overloaded for each element type.
• Step 2 - Each element class implements accept(Visitor v).
• Step 3 - accept() calls back visitor.visit(this) - this is double dispatch.
• Step 4 - A concrete Visitor implements the actual logic for each element type.

expert.content:
Double Dispatch Explained

Java method overloading is resolved at compile time based on the static type of the argument - normally just single dispatch on the object a method is called on. Visitor Pattern achieves double dispatch - the method actually invoked depends on BOTH the runtime type of the element AND the runtime type of the visitor.
• First dispatch - item.accept(visitor) resolves by the actual runtime type of item (Book or Electronics).
• Second dispatch - inside accept(), visitor.visit(this) now has a compile-time-known static type for this (Book or Electronics), so the correct overloaded visit() is picked.
• This two-step trick is how Visitor simulates polymorphic dispatch based on two objects instead of one.

Open/Closed Principle - Adding Operations Without Modifying Classes

To add a new operation (e.g. a DiscountVisitor), you simply create a new class implementing Visitor. The Book and Electronics classes are never touched again - this satisfies the Open/Closed Principle perfectly for adding new operations.

The Tradeoff - Adding New Element Types Is Expensive

Visitor Pattern flips the usual extensibility tradeoff:
• Easy - adding new operations (just write a new Visitor implementation).
• Hard - adding new element types (e.g. a Furniture class) requires adding a new visit(Furniture) method to the Visitor interface AND to every existing concrete visitor.

So Visitor is best used when the set of element classes is stable/rarely changes, but the set of operations performed on them grows frequently.

Real Use - Abstract Syntax Trees (AST) / Compiler Design

• Compilers represent source code as an AST with node types like BinaryExpr, IfStatement, MethodDecl.
• Different phases (type checking, optimization, code generation, pretty-printing) are each implemented as a separate Visitor over the same fixed set of AST node types.
• This keeps each compiler phase in its own class instead of scattering logic across every node class.

Common Mistakes

• Using Visitor when element types change frequently (causes cascading interface changes across every visitor).
• Forgetting to implement accept() consistently on every element subclass.
• Putting mutable state inside the Visitor without resetting it between traversals.

Visitor vs Iterator

AspectVisitorIterator
PurposePerform a type-specific operation on each elementSequentially traverse elements without exposing structure
Adds new behavior?Yes, via new visitor classesNo, only traversal
Element type awarenessVisitor is aware of every concrete element typeIterator is unaware of element types, it just returns items

When NOT to Use Visitor

• When the class hierarchy of elements changes often.
• When there's only one operation ever needed - a simple method on the class is simpler.
• When the double-dispatch complexity isn't worth it for a small, stable set of operations.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Visitor solve?Lets you add new operations to a fixed set of element classes without modifying those classes
What is double dispatch?Method selection based on the runtime types of TWO objects (the element and the visitor) instead of just one, achieved via accept()/visit() calling each other
What's the main tradeoff of Visitor?Adding new operations is easy (new Visitor class); adding new element types is hard (must update the Visitor interface and every existing visitor)
Where is Visitor commonly used in real systems?Compilers/interpreters operating on an Abstract Syntax Tree, where each compiler phase is a separate Visitor
Visitor vs Iterator - what's the difference?Iterator just traverses elements without adding behavior; Visitor performs a type-specific operation on each element it visits

cheatNotes: Design pattern - Proven, reusable solution to a common software design problem.
Gang of Four (GoF) - 23 classic design patterns grouped into 3 categories.
3 categories - Creational, Structural, and Behavioral patterns.
SRP - Single Responsibility: a class should have only one reason to change.
OCP - Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification.
LSP - Liskov Substitution: subtypes must be substitutable for base types.
ISP - Interface Segregation: prefer many small interfaces over one large one.
DIP - Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.
Creational patterns deal with object creation mechanisms.
Singleton - Ensures only ONE instance of a class exists globally.
Singleton: constructor must be private; expose static getInstance().
Eager initialization - Creates the singleton instance at class loading time.
Lazy initialization - Creates the instance only when first requested.
Double-checked locking - Thread-safe lazy singleton with minimal synchronization.
Bill Pugh Singleton - Uses a static inner holder class for lazy, thread-safe init.
Enum Singleton - Most secure form, immune to reflection and serialization attacks.
Override readResolve()/clone() to prevent breaking Singleton via serialization/cloning.
Factory Method - Delegates object creation to subclasses via a factory method.
Abstract Factory - Creates families of related objects without specifying concrete classes.
Builder - Constructs complex objects step-by-step, separating construction from representation.
Prototype - Creates new objects by cloning an existing instance.
Object Pool - Reuses expensive objects from a pool instead of recreating them.
Spring BeanFactory/ApplicationContext - Real-world Factory + Singleton usage.
Structural patterns deal with composing classes/objects into larger structures.
Adapter - Converts one interface into another expected by the client.
Decorator - Adds new behavior to an object dynamically without altering its class.
Facade - Provides a simplified unified interface to a complex subsystem.
Proxy - Provides a placeholder/surrogate to control access to another object.
Composite - Composes objects into tree structures for part-whole hierarchies.
Bridge - Decouples abstraction from implementation so both can vary independently.
Flyweight - Shares common state across many objects to save memory.
java.io.BufferedReader wrapping Reader is a real-world Decorator example.
Behavioral patterns deal with communication and responsibility between objects.
Observer - Notifies dependent objects automatically when subject state changes.
Strategy - Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms, selected at runtime.
Command - Encapsulates a request as an object, enabling undo/queueing.
Iterator - Provides sequential access to elements without exposing internals.
Template Method - Defines an algorithm skeleton, letting subclasses override steps.
State - Allows an object to alter behavior when its internal state changes.
Chain of Responsibility - Passes a request along a chain of handlers.
Mediator - Centralizes complex communication between a set of objects.
Visitor - Separates an algorithm from the object structure it operates on.
java.util.Comparator is a real-world Strategy pattern example.
Java Collections' Iterator interface is a real-world Iterator pattern example.
Avoid large if-else/switch blocks in factories using a Registry Pattern (Map).
Reflection-based factory enables dynamic object creation from class names.
Prefer composition over inheritance when applying Structural/Behavioral patterns.
Overusing patterns adds needless complexity - apply only when the problem fits.
